profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting in an ML research lab between the project lead and the research engineer for the next six-week push on the 'Agentic Design of Compositional Machines' project. The team has already built the BesiegeField benchmark and run early LLM baselines; this meeting is to plan the RL finetuning phase and the internal milestone that will feed a workshop submission update and a lab demo. The agenda is to decide what the next experimental package will include, how the cold-start data and evaluation runs will be prepared, who owns each implementation piece, and what 'ready by the end of the month' means operationally. The expected outcome is a shared-seeming plan for dataset preparation, training runs, evaluation, and an internal report/demo checkpoint.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: LLM evaluation, agentic workflows, benchmark design
members.background: Maya leads a small academic-industry collaboration on embodied reasoning and recently wrote the draft section introducing BesiegeField and the benchmark protocol.
members.private_state: She wants a clean, defensible experimental package that can be shown to collaborators in four weeks without reopening benchmark design debates, and she is worried about accidental benchmark contamination or results that are hard to explain.
hidden_assumptions: When she says 'the benchmark tasks,' she means the fixed held-out evaluation split used in the draft paper, not the broader library of BesiegeField tasks.
A 'working run' is something stable enough to include in the internal results table and replay in front of collaborators, not merely a run that executes end-to-end once.
The 'cold-start set' already includes the necessary formatting and validity checks because the annotation protocol was settled during the previous benchmark phase.
If they 'package a demo,' the environment setup and visualizations are part of the engineering handoff rather than a separate research deliverable.

members.name: Arjun Patel
members.expertise: RL training infrastructure, simulation pipelines, data tooling
members.background: Arjun joined from an applied robotics lab and has been maintaining the BesiegeField simulator wrappers, rollout logging, and job orchestration on the lab cluster.
members.private_state: He wants to keep the plan feasible under cluster limits, avoid overcommitting to polished artifacts before training is stable, and leave room to use more task instances for shaping and stress-testing.
hidden_assumptions: When someone refers to 'the benchmark tasks,' that naturally includes the full curated task pool unless they explicitly say 'held-out split.'
A 'working run' means the training/eval pipeline completes without crashes and produces sensible logs, even if seeds are not yet consistent enough for reporting.
The 'cold-start set' is still a raw asset that needs deduplication, XML validity normalization, and simulator-side filtering before training.
If they 'package a demo,' that means exposing the latest checkpoint through the existing replay UI, while polished setup and presenter-facing materials can come later.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'run on the benchmark tasks' before the milestone.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya means the fixed held-out evaluation split described in the draft: 24 tasks reserved for headline comparison.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arjun means the broader internal benchmark pool of roughly 70 curated tasks that includes the held-out split plus development tasks used for stress-testing and reward shaping checks.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have been using the phrase 'benchmark tasks' for months, and in everyday lab conversation it sounds precise enough that neither expects the other to mean a different task subset.

misalignment_points.topic: What a 'working run' needs to satisfy
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that they need 'at least one working run' by the end of the month.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya means one reproducible training run with reportable evaluation numbers and replays clean enough to show externally.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arjun means one successful end-to-end pipeline execution that trains, saves checkpoints, and completes evaluation jobs without infrastructure failures.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In research meetings, 'working' often functions as an informal progress marker, and both participants assume their operational standard is the obvious one for the milestone.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in 'prepping the cold-start set'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Arjun will 'prep the cold-start set' this week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya believes this means packaging the already-approved examples into training shards and manifest files, because quality checks were effectively completed during data curation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arjun believes this includes additional XML repair, duplicate removal, simulator validity screening, and converting examples into trajectory-ready records before any sharding.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Data preparation sounds like a single routine task, and the omitted substeps feel too implementation-specific to restate unless someone suspects a disagreement.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'package the demo' alongside the results update.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya assumes Arjun will prepare a near-turnkey demo bundle: pinned environment, selected replays, and a simple launch path a collaborator can run on a fresh machine.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arjun assumes he only needs to hook the latest checkpoint into the lab's existing replay interface on the cluster; portability and presenter-facing polish are separate tasks.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are used to saying 'demo' as shorthand for a shareable artifact, but one thinks in terms of external presentation readiness while the other thinks in terms of internal technical accessibility.

turns.inner_thought: I need this next phase to stay tightly scoped. In four weeks I want something I can put in front of collaborators without reopening benchmark design or having to explain away unstable numbers. The draft already frames the held-out evaluation split cleanly, so the RL push should plug into that, not sprawl.
turns.utterance: Okay, let’s use this meeting to lock the next four-to-six-week push. I want the RL finetuning phase to feed an end-of-month internal checkpoint, and that checkpoint should be solid enough to support the collaborator update and the workshop refresh. So today I’d like us to be concrete about what the package includes, what has to happen first, and what we mean by ready.

turns.inner_thought: The main risk is promising polished results before the infrastructure is stable. I should sequence this as pipeline reliability first, then broader runs across the full curated benchmark pool so we can see where training breaks, where reward shaping is weird, and what the cluster can sustain.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From my side, the cleanest plan is to stabilize the training loop first, make sure the jobs behave end to end, and then run on the benchmark tasks before the checkpoint. That should give us a real read on where things stand without front-loading too much polish.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, as long as 'working' means something I can actually cite: reproducible enough to report, with evaluation on the held-out tasks and replays I won’t be embarrassed to show. I do not want a one-off cluster success being treated as milestone-complete.
turns.utterance: Yeah, that sounds right. The main thing I want us aiming at is at least one working run by the end of the month that we can point to in the update, rather than a loose collection of partial pieces.

turns.inner_thought: A working run, to me, is one where the full pipeline actually executes: rollout collection, rewards, checkpoints, eval, logs, no silent failures. If I can get that once, then I can iterate on seed stability afterward. I should describe it in infrastructure terms since that’s the immediate bottleneck.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I’d break that down into getting rollout collection, reward logging, checkpointing, and evaluation to all complete cleanly on cluster jobs. If those pieces hold together, we’ll have at least one working run and a base to build from.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Then Arjun can just package the approved cold-start examples into the manifests and shards so training can start as soon as I settle the config. The formatting and validity checks should already be behind us from the previous benchmark pass.
turns.utterance: Great. Then let’s have you prep the cold-start set this week, so as soon as the config is finalized we can start training without losing another cycle.

turns.inner_thought: That’s fine, but I definitely need to do more than just package it. The cold-start asset is still raw in places: dedupe, XML cleanup, simulator-side validity filtering, then conversion into records the trainer can consume. It’s all part of prep in my book.
turns.utterance: Yep, I can take that. I’ll prep the cold-start set this week and make sure the examples are cleaned up, anything simulator-invalid gets filtered, and the whole thing is in a form the trainer can ingest.

turns.inner_thought: Once the first stable, reportable run lands, I need numbers on the 24 held-out tasks and a handful of clean replays for the write-up. I’m not looking for a giant exploratory dump; I want something defensible and easy to narrate.
turns.utterance: Perfect. And once the first run lands, I want numbers on the benchmark tasks and a few representative replays we can use for the write-up.

turns.inner_thought: I can queue evaluation over the full benchmark pool and then inspect the logs to pick examples that look sane. That’s useful both for stress-testing and for finding decent demos. If the pipeline finishes and the trajectories look reasonable, that’s enough for the first pass.
turns.utterance: That should be straightforward. I can schedule evaluation across the benchmark tasks and then use those logs to choose examples that look sensible.

turns.inner_thought: I also want the demo bundle moving in parallel, because collaborators shouldn’t have to wait for a separate engineering sprint. Ideally they can get a pinned environment, selected replays, and a simple launch path shortly after the results update.
turns.utterance: Also, let’s package the demo in parallel with the results update so collaborators can try the machine-building agent soon after we circulate numbers.

turns.inner_thought: Sure—once the run is working, I can expose the latest checkpoint through the existing replay UI on the cluster. That gets people access quickly. I’m not going to commit right now to a fresh-machine setup or polished presenter materials before training settles.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. Once the run is working and the outputs are easy to inspect, I’ll wire the latest checkpoint into the replay UI so we can package the demo alongside the update.

turns.inner_thought: So Arjun owns the operational path end to end: prep the cold-start data, get training going, evaluate on the held-out benchmark split, and produce the demo bundle. I’ll handle the narrative and make sure the draft tables and framing are ready once his pieces arrive.
turns.utterance: Okay, let me summarize so we stay aligned: you’ll prep the cold-start set, get training running, do the benchmark-task evaluation, and package the demo; I’ll handle the experimental narrative, the write-up framing, and the collaborator-facing update around that.

turns.inner_thought: That timeline is workable if the cluster behaves. By end of week I should have the data prep done in my sense and at least one full pipeline pass, even if it’s not yet stable enough for external reporting. I’ll send a status that emphasizes progress without overpromising polish.
turns.utterance: Yep, that works for me. I’ll send an end-of-week status once data prep and the first pipeline pass are done, and then we can see how close we are to the end-of-month checkpoint.
